chapter_theme: Civakan leaves Padumai, crosses the forest and mountain singing a hymn to the Jina on the fruit of deeds, the soul and the bond of love, and at a hermitage of Vaishnava forest ascetics answers their discourse by mocking their diet, fires, bathing and matted hair with the beasts that already live so, then sets out knowledge, right vision and right conduct as what ends deeds.

cast.role: the hero, son of Vijayai, travelling alone after leaving Padumai
the Jina, Lord of the asoka tree, addressed in Civakan's hymn (1418-1420)
the forest ascetics of the hermitage, who keep the way of Kama's father and debate with Civakan

1412.reading: Vijayai's son, whose generous hand gives like the rain cloud and whose fresh garland drips honey, leaves the woman of musk-scented hair to pine and takes on foot to the harsh forest.
1412.event: Civakan sets out alone on foot into the forest, leaving Padumai grieving.
1412.nuance: The verb வழங்கும் returns in each line (the hand that gives, the garland that sheds honey, the hair that sheds musk, the forest he walks), so the line-by-line play binds his generosity, his finery and her grief to the walk into the wilds.

1413.reading: The strong hero, the weariness of love with women whose chastity holds like a string on a bow now passing, heads gladly for the mountain forest.
1413.event: Civakan, refreshed from the fatigue of love, presses on toward the hill forest.
1413.nuance: Line 3 (முலைகொள் கண்கள் கண்ணின் எழுதி முள்கும்) is hard to construe; it seems to recall his love-play with the wives, but the exact sense is not fixed. The bowstring simile praises the wives' karpu as something that never leaves them, even as he leaves.

1414.reading: In a forest of fruiting plantains, as langurs and monkeys with faces like smeared black wax scatter, the prince looks about to ease his sorrow, and ahead of him a thicket appears like a sea ringed with cold white waves.
1414.event: Civakan walks on through the plantain forest and sees a grove ahead.

1415.reading: Like women of fragrant hair who embrace their drinkers and cast them off when the gain runs out, the swarming bees cling to a flowering branch until it bends, drink its honey and drone nearby, while the noble one walks slowly on.
1415.event: Civakan walks slowly through the flowering grove.
1415.nuance: The landscape is read through a moral simile: the bees are the courtesans who leave a man once his wealth is gone.

1416.reading: He reaches the mountain by a path that rises like the minds of the rich, is dark as the hearts of the wealthy, sheds pollen sweetly, winds like a deadly snake, and narrows the further one goes, like friendship with the small.
1416.event: Civakan climbs the narrowing path to the mountain.
1416.nuance: All four similes are moral: the pride and inner darkness of the rich and the dwindling friendship of petty men. The last is the didactic books' image of a bond that shrinks over time, set to a path.

1417.reading: The mountain, its pools as eyes and its kuvalai flowers as eyes, seems to pity the youth's matchless form and weep with its falls; he bathes gladly in the cascade, crowns himself with buds and sings to the Lord.
1417.event: Civakan bathes in a mountain waterfall, garlands himself and begins a hymn to the Jina.

1418.reading: Civakan praises the Lord of the cool flowering asoka for teaching that the fruit of the two kinds of deed travels to the one who did them and that no other receives it, and worships him if this is his word.
1418.event: Civakan sings the first verse of a hymn to the Jina of the asoka tree.

claims.claim: the fruit of good and evil deeds reaches the one who did them, and no other receives it

1418.nuance: The refrain பூம்பிண்டிக் கோமான் names the Jina by the asoka (பிண்டி) under which he sits. The hymn's conditional form ('if this is the nature of your word') makes each doctrine the ground of worship, and the doctrine of the first verse is the one Civakan will use against the ascetics: no rite done by the body can carry off a deed's fruit.

1419.reading: He praises the Lord of the asoka, which spreads four kaathams bearing garlands loud with bees, for declaring that the soul exists, known by its own nature when one inquires, and that the soul is not from anything other than itself.

claims.claim: the soul exists and is known by its own nature
the soul does not arise from any other thing

1419.nuance: Line 2 is garbled in the text (உண்டாய வ்வவுயிரே); read as உண்டாய அவ்வுயிரே, it says the soul is not produced from another thing, which sets the hymn against those who make the soul a product of the elements.

1420.reading: He praises the Lord of the asoka, over which honey drips and bees roam among the hanging garlands, for teaching both that by love the eight karmas pass and that, because it is still love, the eight karmas do not pass.

claims.claim: love directed to the right end helps wear away the eight karmas, yet as attachment it cannot itself end them

1420.nuance: The verse is a deliberate paradox, and its sense turns on காதல், which may be love of the Jina or of the path, and on மறைதி, 'you declared' or 'you hid'. Read either way, even devotion is counted as a bond: the eight karmas (எண்வினை) are the Jain reckoning of the kinds of karma.

1421.reading: Having praised thus sweetly and walked round in reverence, he goes on alone and comes upon a cool flowering grove where forest ascetics live, a sages' retreat like Chitrakuta.
1421.event: Civakan circumambulates the shrine and reaches the ascetics' hermitage.
1421.nuance: முனிவர் சித்திர கூடம் முன்னாது may compare the grove to Chitrakuta, Rama's forest of sages, or say that he went on not thinking of it; the comparison is taken here.

1422.reading: He reaches the dwelling of those who eat only clean food: grass, lotus stamens, rice of the tall bamboo, wild grains grown in water, sweet fruits, green fruits and roots.
1422.event: Civakan enters the hermitage of the forest ascetics.
1422.nuance: The list of foods is set out with care because Civakan will argue from it (1429, 1430): if such diet burned deeds, the beasts of the forest would be freed.

1423.reading: They are men of hard vows who stand amid the five fires to win release, whose tongues have recited the Veda at length, and whose minds are set on the fire rite without discernment.
1423.nuance: The five fires (ஆரழல் ஐந்து) are the four fires round the ascetic and the sun above. தெரிவில் may be the narrator's judgment, 'without discernment', or mean only 'chosen'; if the first, the Jain poet has already weighed them before the debate.

1424.reading: Those of generous heart bring him sweet nectar of the valli root and clear sweet fruit of the mountain plantain and, bidding the noble guest feast, tend him gladly.
1424.event: The ascetics feed Civakan with roots and fruit as their guest.

1425.reading: The great ascetics beside him, judging that this youth like the white moon is deep in learning and has heard the true doctrine, resolve to measure him too and recite one or two of their lofty discourses.
1425.event: The ascetics test Civakan with a few discourses of their own.

1426.reading: When the elders had spoken, the noble one answered that if a man who swims the sea with a mountain strapped to him could be saved, then all who are bound here by attachment would be saved as well.
1426.event: Civakan begins his reply to the ascetics with the image of a man swimming the sea under a mountain.

claims.claim: one who keeps his attachments cannot cross the sea of births

1426.nuance: தொடர்ப்பாடு (bond, attachment) is taken as the mountain on the swimmer's back; the image prepares the charge (1432 to 1434) that these ascetics have carried their households into the forest.

1427.reading: Growing great matted hair in search of release, wrapping the body in cloth, carrying a white skull as a bowl and wearing bark: these, he says, are said to be seeds of a mean birth.

claims.claim: the ascetic's marks of matted hair, garb and skull bowl do not bring release but sow further birth

1427.nuance: என்பவே ('so it is said') rests the judgment on authority rather than argument; the argument comes in 1429 to 1434. The verse does not say the marks are merely useless but that they seed a lowly birth.

1428.reading: The ascetic replies: which is the safe good path? We too are resolved on that path of purity; young bull, if there is any evil in the way of Kama's father, tell it.
1428.event: An ascetic challenges Civakan to show any fault in their Vaishnava way.

claims.claim: the way of Kama's father that we follow is the safe and pure path

1428.nuance: காமன் தாதை, Kama's father, is Vishnu, so the ascetics name their path as his, though their practices (the five fires, the Veda, the fire rite of 1423) are those of Vedic forest ascetics. The claim is refuted in Civakan's answer, 1429 to 1436, and the ascetics' conversion in 1437.

1429.reading: If, he says, the Lord told you that unfit deeds do not stay with those who eat the fruits that hang ripening from the trees, then the bat with its folded wings, hanging from tall trees and eating the fruit nearby, would shed its old deeds.

claims.claim: living on hanging fruit removes evil deeds, as the Lord taught
a diet of fruit does not destroy old deeds, or the bat would be freed

1429.nuance: Each of the next verses has the same form: the ascetics' practice is stated as a conditional and answered with a forest creature that already lives that way. பகவனார் (the Lord) is the ascetics' god as Civakan quotes them.

1430.reading: If eating lotus stamens and grass and standing amid the five fires in the prescribed way cuts off cruel deeds, then all the forest doves, which eat grit and burn in the heat, would conquer their binding deeds and put them to flight.

claims.claim: eating grass and standing amid the five fires cuts off cruel deeds
bodily mortification and diet do not conquer deeds, or the dove would be freed

1431.reading: If, with long matted hair, plunging in water, lying on the ground and a wasted body, you would win the highest state, then the bear that roams the forest, plunges into pools and stands in the wild would have to win release; give up empty words, he says.

claims.claim: matted hair, ritual bathing, sleeping on the ground and wasting the body win the highest state
bathing and bodily hardship do not yield release, or the bear would gain it

1432.reading: If leaving the soft beds of women of artful speech for the bare ground of a leaf hut, while still embracing their breasts there, breaks all one's deeds, then, he says, the deeds of the hill kuravar would perish too.

claims.claim: a forest life that keeps its wives is no renunciation and breaks no deeds

1432.nuance: The ascetics are householders in the forest: they have left the palace bed, not the wife. The kuravar, who live just so in leaf huts on the hill, make the point that a change of bed is not a change of life; 1437 has the converts put away their households.

1433.reading: Can bright blood that has fallen on white cloth and stained it be washed out with blood? So can the sin born of clinging to sweet-voiced women be removed by union with women?

claims.claim: sin born of desire for women cannot be removed while one keeps lying with women

1433.nuance: The image is of washing a stain with the same stuff that made it: the remedy must be other in kind than the fault.

1434.reading: If one wraps fire in fine cloth for fear of its burning and hides it away, will the fierce flame not burn? So one who leaves the guarded house of women for the forest, but carries the sin of old deeds, cannot wear it away by wishing to.

claims.claim: going to the forest does not wear away old sin that one carries within

1434.nuance: Lines 2 and 4 are rhetorical questions in -ஆமே, and the second half of line 4 (பறைக்குற்றாற் பறைக்கலாமே) is hard to construe; it is read as 'can one wear it away merely by setting out to?'. The fire hidden in cloth is the old deed carried into the forest.

1435.reading: Do not gaze on pleasure like a sick old monkey, he says; this body will drop at once like a ripe fruit from its stalk; practise austerity in the bamboo forest in the form of the Conqueror and go to drink the joy of the ripe heaven: strive for that.

claims.claim: the body falls soon like ripe fruit, so one must not linger in pleasure
austerity done in the Jina's form leads to the joys of heaven

1435.nuance: Civakan does not reject austerity: he keeps it, in the Jina's form (வென்றான் உருவொடு), and promises heaven (துறக்கம்) rather than release, the nearer fruit; release comes only with the three jewels of 1436.

1436.reading: Knowledge is discerning things as they truly are; right vision is trusting without falsehood the things so made clear; conduct is withering the five senses and living without wearing down any soul; when all three are full in this way, he says, both kinds of deed pass away.

claims.claim: knowledge, right vision and right conduct together, each made full, end both good and evil deeds
right conduct is restraint of the five senses and not harming any living being

1436.nuance: These are the Jain three jewels, named here ஞானம், காட்சி and ஒழுக்கம். The weight falls on மூன்றும் and நிறைந்த: no one of them, and none in part, is enough. The answer to the ascetics is not less austerity but a different cause of release, in which conduct is defined by non-harm (உயிரைத் தேயாது).

links.note: Civakan's hymn praises the Jina for teaching that a deed's fruit reaches its doer and no other; the Manimekalai names fierce vow-keepers who hold that a deed reaches its doer even without intention, and tells of a seat built to answer them.
links.teaches: Seen from the Buddhist epic, the doctrine the Cintamani's hymn takes for granted has a disputed edge, whether a deed done without intention still binds, which the Jain hymn never raises.

links.note: The hymn says the soul is not from anything other than itself; the Neelakesi's sage asks whether a child is the body, made of the parents' blood, or the soul, which came to a human birth by its own former deed.
links.teaches: The Neelakesi spells out what the Cintamani's brief formula denies: the soul is not produced by the parents or the elements but brings itself into each birth by its own deeds.

links.note: The Kural bids one cling to the one free of clinging in order to let clinging go; the Cintamani's hymn says love wears the karmas away and yet, being love, cannot end them.
links.teaches: The couplet makes attachment to the unattached the way out of attachment, while the Jain hymn admits that very attachment and counts it still a bond, so the two disagree on whether devotion can itself be the final cause of freedom, on the reading of காதல் as love of the Jina.

gains.a: a sharp foil showing that its paradox denies what the couplet affirms, devotion as the last step to freedom
gains.b: an objection the couplet does not face, that clinging to the unattached remains a clinging

links.note: The Kural says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; Civakan says matted hair, robes and the skull bowl are seeds of a mean birth.
links.teaches: Where the couplet sets the marks aside as unnecessary, the epic counts them as harmful, sowing rebirth, so the pair shows two degrees of the same critique of outward signs.

gains.a: a neutral maxim that makes plain how much further its own judgment goes
gains.b: a case where the marks are not merely superfluous but are taken for the path itself and so mislead

links.note: Pattinathar calls vows, Vedas, Agamas, fire rites, offerings, mantras and pujas all pretence; Civakan mocks standing in the five fires and eating grass, but goes on to urge austerity in the Jina's form (1435).
links.teaches: Both reject the Vedic ascetic's fire and diet, but the Siddhar rejects observance as such, while the Jain hero rejects one school's austerities only to set up his own, so the pairing separates a critique of ritual from a rivalry of disciplines.

gains.a: a contrast that shows its polemic is not anti-ritual in general, since it keeps tapas
gains.b: a reasoned reductio, the beast that already lives the practice, where the Siddhar only lists and dismisses

links.note: Civakan says that if plunging in water won release the bear would gain it; Tirumular says the holy waters are within the heart, and those who do not bathe there so their deeds perish wander the land.
links.teaches: Both deny that outer bathing destroys deeds, but Tirumular keeps the bath and moves it inward, while the Jain hero drops it and replaces it with knowledge, vision and conduct, so the two show different ways out of the same criticism.

gains.a: an inward alternative its own mockery does not offer, which shows its answer is substitution rather than interiorization
gains.b: a blunt test, the bear in the pool, for the outward bathing its verse dismisses

links.note: Pattinathar asks what forest life, eating wind, rags and the bowl avail without inner love, and says the Lord's true lovers reach release even living at home beside their women; Civakan says sin born of desire for women cannot be removed by union with women.
links.teaches: The two agree that going to the forest is nothing in itself, but they part on the household: the Saiva poet lets love free one beside one's wife, while the Jain hero makes leaving the wife a condition, so the shared attack on outward renunciation hides opposite views of the married life.

gains.a: a rival conclusion from the same premise, which shows that its demand to leave women is a doctrine of its own and not implied by its critique
gains.b: the strongest objection to its claim, that sin born of desire cannot be cleansed while desire continues

links.note: The Neelakesi praises those who leave home for forest and hill and strive with knowledge to wear away their deeds; Civakan says leaving the house of women for the forest does not wear away old sin carried within.
links.teaches: Read together, the two Jain epics place the cause of release not in the forest but in the knowledge the Neelakesi names (ஞானமொடு), which the Cintamani's ascetics lack until Civakan supplies it in 1436.

links.note: Civakan says the body will drop at once like a ripe fruit from its stalk; the Naladiyar warns that a harsh wind can drop the green fruit while the ripe stays on the tree.
links.teaches: The epic's ripe fruit makes death a ripening that comes in order, but the quatrain's fallen green fruit warns that it need not wait for age, and the two urgings to act now rest on different pictures of when the body falls.

gains.a: a caution that its own image of ripeness understates the danger to the young
gains.b: a renouncer's use of the falling fruit that turns the urge to do good into a call to austerity

links.note: The Kural says one whose mind ponders and knows what is with certainty need not think again of birth; Civakan says knowledge, right vision and right conduct must all three be full before both kinds of deed pass.
links.teaches: Where the couplet lets true knowing alone end rebirth, the Jain formula makes knowing only one of three and insists on vision and conduct of non-harm as well, so the pair shows the Kural's chapter on true knowledge as a narrower account of release.

gains.a: a single-cause claim against which its insistence on all three, each made full, stands out
gains.b: a fuller account of what knowing must be joined with before birth ends, which the couplet leaves unsaid

source_issues: 1414, 1415, 1418-1420, 1429-1431 and 1434-1436 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build; the joins read correctly.
1419 line 2 reads உண்டாய வ்வவுயிரே, apparently garbled for உண்டாய அவ்வுயிரே.
1420 line 3 திவண்டுலாங் looks like a misprint, perhaps for திவண்டு உலாம்; the sense is not affected.
1434 line 4 பறைக்குற்றாற் பறைக்கலாமே is hard to construe and may be corrupt.
